source_text: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

nodes.content: Human beings are psychologically determined by sensory experiences, with pain and pleasure serving as the exclusive masters governing all actions, thoughts, and words.
nodes.source_quote: Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure. They alone point out what we ought to do and determine what we shall do...

nodes.content: The moral standard for all action (including private conduct and government measures) is the Principle of Utility, which assesses actions based solely on their consequences for increasing or lessening happiness.
nodes.source_quote: By 'the principle of utility' is meant the principle that approves or disapproves of every action according to the tendency it appears to have to increase or lessen—i.e. to promote or oppose—the happiness of the person or group whose interest is in question.

nodes.content: Pleasure and immunity from pain are the only things that possess intrinsic value or are considered goods; pain is the only intrinsic evil.
nodes.source_quote: Now, pleasure is in itself a good; indeed it's the only good if we set aside immunity from pain; and pain is in itself an evil, and without exception the only evil; or else 'good' and 'evil' have no meaning!

nodes.content: Moral judgment must be objective, resting on a measurable calculation of consequences (the greatest happiness of the greatest number), and must reject principles based on subjective feelings like moral sense or caprice.
nodes.source_quote: The Principle of Sympathy and Antipathy 'is not so much a positive principle as a term employed to signify the negation of all principle.'

nodes.content: Motives and dispositions are not inherently good or bad; their moral quality is entirely derivative, judged by the goodness or badness of the resulting intentions and material consequences.
nodes.source_quote: ...there is no such thing as a sort of motive that is in itself a bad one.

nodes.content: Legislation (the art of government) and private ethics share the singular objective of maximizing the community's happiness, differing only in the means used to direct conduct.
nodes.source_quote: Private ethics has happiness for its goal, and legislation can have no other.

nodes.content: Utility (or Happiness): The property of tending to produce overall pleasure or prevent overall pain, benefit, or good for the affected party. It is the universal and absolute standard of right and wrong.
nodes.source_quote: By 'utility' is meant the property of something whereby it tends •to produce benefit, advantage, pleasure, good, or happiness. . . or. . . •to prevent the happening of mischief, pain, evil, or unhappiness to the party whose interest is considered.

nodes.content: Prudence: The ethical duty of pursuing the parts of one's own behavior that affect the interests of oneself alone (duty to oneself).
nodes.source_quote: The quality that shows up in the discharge of this branch of duty (if 'duty' is the right word) is prudence.

nodes.content: Probity: The negative duty component of a man's duty to his neighbor, specifically avoiding actions that lessen the neighbor's happiness.
nodes.source_quote: Discharging the negative duty is probity...

nodes.content: Beneficence: The positive duty component of a man's duty to his neighbor, actively seeking to increase the neighbor's happiness.
nodes.source_quote: ...discharging the positive duty is beneficence.

nodes.content: Consistency: The systematic adherence to one chosen principle (Utility) without self-contradiction, necessary for rational moral or political decision-making.
nodes.source_quote: Such is the stuff that man is made of: in principle and in practice, on the right path or a wrong one, the rarest of all human qualities is consistency.

nodes.content: Frugality: A property desired in punishment, ensuring that the punishment does not produce superfluous and needless pain.
nodes.source_quote: Frugality, therefore, is a sixth property to be wished for in a mode of punishment.

nodes.content: Systematic/Architectural: Dedicated to building a comprehensive, ordered, and integrated structure for knowledge, viewing the entire legal system as an edifice based on foundational principles.
nodes.source_quote: Planning his entire body of work to cover all branches of legislation (civil, penal, procedure, constitutional, international). Uses the metaphor of building 'the edifice of happiness built by the hands of reason and of law'.

nodes.content: Quantitative/Calculative: Applies a methodical, mathematical approach to moral problems, assuming that all elements of ethical evaluation can be broken down and assigned a measurable value.
nodes.source_quote: Developing the elaborate system of the 'felicific calculus' by listing seven quantifiable circumstances for measuring pleasure and pain.

nodes.content: Analytical/Conceptual: Highly focused on linguistic precision and distinguishing concepts (like motive, intention, and disposition) that are often conflated in common discourse.
nodes.source_quote: Providing extensive sections explaining the subtle but crucial difference between the goodness/badness of an intention (consequences aimed at) and the goodness/badness of a motive (cause of the intention).

nodes.content: Censorial/Reformative: Adopts a critical stance toward existing institutions and traditional legal terminology, aiming to correct and articulate what law ought to be (censorial jurisprudence).
nodes.source_quote: Criticizing systems like 'common law' and 'judiciary law' as mere 'fictitious composition'. Openly challenges deeply held prejudices.

nodes.content: Exhaustive/Dichotomous: Demonstrates a drive toward complete coverage by dividing subjects recursively into exactly two parts (bisection), believing this 'exhaustive method' is essential for producing genuine philosophical advances.
nodes.source_quote: Applying the exhaustive method to the classification of offences, starting by splitting mischief by identifiability of sufferers, leading eventually to five exhaustive classes.

nodes.content: Empirical/Psychological: Grounds moral and legal theory in observable human experience (psychology or 'moral physiology') and the facts of human motivation rather than abstract duties or metaphysical entities.
nodes.source_quote: Building the entire system of sanctions (political, moral, religious, physical) on the single observation that 'there is nothing by which a man can ultimately be made to do something... except pain or pleasure'.

nodes.content: Maximize the Net Happiness of the Community: To establish the necessary principles and calculations that ensure the overall collective well-being is the final arbiter of right action.
nodes.source_quote: The general object that all laws have or ought to have in common is to increase the total happiness of the community...

nodes.content: Provide Rules for the Proportioning of Punishment: To articulate a set of rational, quantifiable rules ensuring that the severity and quality of legal punishment are optimally adjusted to the nature of the offence.
nodes.source_quote: Subservient to these four objectives [of penal law] must be the rules governing the proportion of punishments to offences.

nodes.content: Delineate the Boundary Between Law and Morality: To clearly define the limits of direct coercive legislation, ensuring the law does not intervene where intervention would be ineffective, unprofitable, or groundless.
nodes.source_quote: Every act that promises to be pernicious on the whole to the community... each individual ought to abstain from; but it is not every such act that the legislator ought to compel him to abstain from.

nodes.content: Create a Universal and Natural System of Jurisprudence: To establish a conceptual classification of actions and laws based on universal principles (pain and pleasure) rather than local customs or technical language.
nodes.source_quote: A natural arrangement governed by a principle that is recognised by all men will serve for the jurisprudence of all nations. . . the •matter serves as a standard by which they might be tested.

nodes.content: Utility: The property of anything that tends to produce benefit, pleasure, good, or happiness, or to prevent pain, mischief, or evil for the party concerned. It is the measure of moral rightness.
nodes.source_quote: By 'utility' is meant the property of something whereby it tends •to produce benefit, advantage, pleasure, good, or happiness (all equivalent in the present case)...

nodes.content: Mischief: The aggregate of harmful actual or probable consequences of an act, resulting in pain or loss of pleasure. It quantifies the evil an act causes and is the sole target the penal law is designed to exclude or prevent.
nodes.source_quote: The tendency of an act is harmful when its actual or probable consequences are harmful; and the harmful consequences of an act whose tendency is harmful can be thought of as constituting one aggregate item that we could call the mischief of the act.

nodes.content: Sanction: A source of obligatory power or motives, consisting of pain and pleasure, which binds a person to observe a rule of conduct. Types include physical, political, moral, and religious sanctions.
nodes.source_quote: Because the pleasures and pains belonging to each of them can give a binding force to any law or rule of conduct, they can all be called 'sanctions'.

nodes.content: Fecundity: A circumstance influencing the value of a pleasure or pain, defined as the chance of the sensation being followed by subsequent sensations of the same kind (pleasure followed by more pleasure, or pain by more pain).
nodes.source_quote: its fecundity, i.e. its chance of being followed by sensations of the same kind (pleasure by pleasure, pain by pain)

nodes.content: Purity: A circumstance influencing the value of a pleasure or pain, defined as the chance of the sensation not being followed by sensations of the opposite kind (pleasure followed by pain, or pain by pleasure).
nodes.source_quote: its purity, i.e. its chance of not being followed by sensations of the opposite kind (pleasure by pain, pain by pleasure).

nodes.content: Intentionality: The state of the will with respect to an act itself or its consequences, indicating whether the agent aimed at producing them. It determines the consequences for which the agent is morally responsible.
nodes.source_quote: the agent's intention or will may be directed either at •the act itself or at •its consequences; and the one the intention aims at may be called 'intentional'—an 'intentional act' or 'intentional consequences'.

nodes.content: Motive: Anything that influences the will, fundamentally consisting of pleasure or pain operating in prospect, which serves as the underlying cause of an intention.
nodes.source_quote: A motive is substantially nothing more than pleasure or pain, operating in a certain manner.

nodes.content: Disposition: A latent or permanent state of mind, inferred from the consistency between a person's motives and intentions, that expresses how apt he is to perform harmful or beneficial acts.
nodes.source_quote: Now a disposition is a kind of fictitious entity, invented for the convenience of discourse in order to express what is thought to be permanent in a man's frame of mind...

nodes.content: Principle of Sympathy and Antipathy: The doctrine that moral approval or disapproval should be based entirely on one's own feelings toward an act, without consulting external considerations like utility. Bentham criticizes this as being a negation of all principle.
nodes.source_quote: By 'the principle of sympathy and antipathy' I mean the principle that approves or disapproves of certain actions not •because of their tending to increase or lessen the happiness... but merely •because a man finds himself disposed to approve or disapprove of them...

edges.explanation: The sensory/psychological bedrock (pain and pleasure as sovereign masters) SUPPORTS the Principle of Utility by establishing the material against which all moral evaluation must be measured.
The Principle of Utility REQUIRES the belief that pleasure and immunity from pain are the only intrinsic goods, as these are the only entities by which happiness can be defined and measured.
The belief that only pleasure/pain have intrinsic value SUPPORTS the rejection of moral systems based on arbitrary sentiment or subjective rules.
The belief that motives are not inherently good or bad reinforces the system's consequentialism, ensuring moral evaluation focuses on the predictable effect of an act rather than the intrinsic cause.
The shared objective of legislation and private ethics (maximizing happiness) PRECEDES the determination of the boundary between legal control and purely moral control.
The motive (expectation of specific pleasure or pain) is the cause that generates the intention (the act of willing the consequences).
To determine utility, one must strictly follow the felicific calculus procedure of balancing pleasures and pains, which includes measuring fecundity and purity.
To determine utility, one must calculate both fecundity (same-kind sensations) and purity (opposite-kind sensations) of pleasures and pains.
Intentionality and consciousness support the inference of disposition - a man's long-term harmful or beneficent tendencies are inferred by observing the intentionality surrounding his actions.

Mischief of the offence PRECEDES punishment - punishment (which is itself mischief) should only be inflicted if there is an existing or threatened mischief greater than the evil of the punishment itself.
The political sanction (laws enforced by government) directly causes the evil of coercion, felt by citizens who obey the law by restraining themselves from otherwise desired acts (prudence).
Frugality supports maximizing net utility by minimizing the cost (reducing real pain inflicted by punishment) while exemplarity maximizes deterrence through apparent pain.
The Principle of Sympathy and Antipathy (subjective feelings as moral basis) directly CONTRADICTS the requirement for objective, measurable calculation of consequences based on utility.
Bentham's quantitative/calculative methodological trait directly supports his development of utility as a measurable concept requiring the felicific calculus.
